title: Vodka
lead: The clean slate of the back bar: what it’s made from, how bottles differ, and how guests order it.

sections.name: What vodka is

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Vodka is meant to taste clean.

know: Any Base works: wheat, rye, corn, potatoes, even grapes.
High Proof off the still, then usually no aging: clean and clear.
37.5% is the EU minimum strength for vodka.
sections.source: EU spirit drinks regulation 2019/787, Annex I (eur-lex.europa.eu)

sections.name: How vodka tastes

lines.label: In short
lines.text: The base leaves a small mark.

know: Wheat vodkas tend to be soft and a little sweet.
Rye is drier, with a peppery edge.
Flavored vodkas add fruit, citrus or vanilla.
sections.source: EU spirit drinks regulation 2019/787, Annex I (eur-lex.europa.eu); Common bar practice

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Usually with a mixer, sometimes up.

Well is our house pour when no brand is named.
Call means they named the bottle. Ring in that one.
Up means chilled, strained, no ice, in a stemmed glass.

lines.label: In short

read.bigIdea: Vodka is meant to taste clean.
read.where: Vodka can be made from **any farm base**: wheat, rye, corn, potatoes, even grapes. It’s distilled to a **high strength** and usually **not aged**, so it comes out clear and clean. In the EU it’s bottled at **37.5% or more**.
read.mixup: Clear doesn’t always mean vodka. **Blanco tequila** and **white rum** are clear too, but they taste of **agave** and **cane**.
read.sayIt: Vodka’s the cleanest spirit on the bar, so the other flavors lead.

keyPoints.line: vodkas tend to be soft and a little sweet.
is drier, with a peppery edge.
vodkas add fruit, citrus or vanilla.

read.bigIdea: The base leaves a small mark.
read.where: Vodka is meant to be neutral, but what it’s made from still shows a little. Words a guest understands: **clean**, **smooth**, **crisp**, **soft**. **Flavored vodkas** add fruit, citrus or vanilla.
read.mixup: A **citrus vodka** is still vodka. **Gin** is the one that has to taste of **juniper**.
read.sayIt: This one’s made from rye, so it’s a little drier and spicier.

read.bigIdea: Usually with a mixer, sometimes up.
read.where: Most vodka orders are **vodka and a mixer**: soda, tonic, cranberry or juice. “Vodka soda” with no brand gets the **well** vodka. If the guest names the bottle, it’s a **call**: get the **brand** right. A **vodka martini** is vodka and dry vermouth, served **up**, and guests order it **dry**, **dirty** or **with a twist**, like a gin one.
read.mixup: “**Vodka soda**” gets our well vodka. “**Tito’s and soda**” is a call: ring in the bottle they named.
read.sayIt: Soda, tonic or cranberry with that?

read.bigIdea: Vodka lets the other ingredients lead.
read.where: Because vodka is clean, the **other ingredients** set the taste. The **Moscow Mule** is vodka, lime and ginger beer. The **Espresso Martini** is vodka, fresh espresso and coffee liqueur. The **Cosmopolitan** is citrus vodka, orange liqueur, lime and cranberry. The **Bloody Mary** is vodka and tomato juice with lemon and spice. The **White Russian** is vodka, coffee liqueur and cream.
read.mixup: A **Moscow Mule** is vodka and ginger beer. With dark rum instead, it’s a **Dark ’n’ Stormy**.
read.sayIt: It’s vodka, so it’s clean: the fruit does the talking.

sources: EU spirit drinks regulation 2019/787, Annex I (eur-lex.europa.eu); Common bar practice; Our book: the classic and house cocktail specs in this app. Facts taken from the Level 2 lessons, which cite them. Written for Mise, Nov 12, 2026.

unverified: Taste words (“soft”, “peppery”, “grassy”) are general bar descriptions, not from a rule. Bar lead to check them against our bottles.
How guests order (mixers, neat or on the rocks, shots) is common US bar usage, not a rule; bar lead to confirm the house wording.
